red.focus: Connect legal remedies to the problem they should solve
red.summary: A remedy may repay a loss, stop harmful conduct, or change future incentives. Learn to identify which outcome the client needs rather than assuming the largest payment is best.
checklist: I can identify compensatory and preventive goals
I can distinguish a remedy from a public fine
I can ask whether relief can be enforced

sections.title: Repair and Prevention Are Different
sections.body_md: A worker injured by an unsafe machine may need compensation for medical costs and action to prevent another injury. A damages award and a safety order can address those needs differently. A public fine may deter misconduct but not automatically pay the injured person. The legal system determines which remedies are available and to whom. Economic analysis helps ask whether the remedy changes incentives, while the lawyer must still identify the governing authority, conditions and procedural route.

sections.title: Incentives Shape Future Conduct
sections.body_md: If the expected cost of an unsafe practice is low because detection is rare, a business may underinvest in prevention. Enforcement, inspections and liability can alter that calculation. But the point is not to assume everyone acts only for money; professional values, reputation and concern for others matter. A sound policy analysis examines real behavior as well as the formal penalty. Legal remedies should protect people effectively, not merely look severe in a statute book.

sections.title: Choose Relief the Institution Can Give
sections.body_md: A tribunal may grant money but lack the power to supervise a factory's future operations. Another agency may impose preventive standards but not resolve a private claim. A legal adviser should match the client's objective to authorized remedies and the institution capable of enforcing them. The strongest theoretical result is useless if it cannot be obtained or implemented. The learner's habit is to ask what the law permits and whether the resulting order will change the real problem.

yellow.focus: Compare liability, regulation and risk-based charges
yellow.summary: Legal systems can reduce harmful externalities through several institutions. Learn why a payment mechanism and a safety standard may work differently and cannot be evaluated by price alone.
checklist: I can identify a tax or charge designed to reflect external cost
I can distinguish ex ante regulation from ex post liability
I can compare monitoring and information costs

sections.title: A Price on External Harm
sections.body_md: A government might charge for pollution to encourage firms to reduce emissions when doing so costs less than the charge. Economists often call a corrective charge Pigouvian when it aims to reflect marginal external harm. Setting the right amount requires evidence about damage and behavior. A tax or fee does not itself prove every private injury is compensable, and its legality depends on public authority. The mechanism is one policy option, not a universal solution to every kind of harm.

sections.title: Standards and Liability Differ in Time
sections.body_md: A safety regulation can require precautions before an accident occurs. A liability rule may assign costs after a legally recognized wrong. Ex ante prevention can be important where injury is irreversible; ex post compensation can support individualized redress but may be slow or hard to collect. A thoughtful comparison considers who holds relevant information, how easily conduct can be monitored, and whether victims can bring claims. The legal order may use both mechanisms together.

sections.title: No Tool Is Costless
sections.body_md: Inspectors require resources, firms may resist reporting, and litigation can consume time and money. A highly detailed permit system can create administrative burdens; a pure damages system may fail when victims cannot prove causation. The right policy depends on the actual risk and institutional capacity. Economic efficiency can inform the choice but cannot supersede binding rights or distribute risk unfairly simply because it is cheaper to do so.

orange.focus: Evaluate remedy design under uncertainty and imperfect enforcement
orange.summary: Advanced economic analysis compares the likelihood of detection, cost of compliance and distribution of losses. Understand why theoretical optimal penalties may fail when institutions and actors are not ideal.
checklist: I can explain how detection probabilities affect incentives
I can analyze distributional effects of remedial policy

sections.title: Detection Probability Changes Behavior
sections.body_md: A penalty of one hundred dollars may have little effect if violations are almost never detected. A policy model can consider expected sanction as probability of detection multiplied by sanction magnitude, while real behavior depends on reputation, norms and risk perception too. Raising penalties without improving detection may be ineffective or disproportionate. The legal analyst must examine statutory limits, safeguards against error and whom enforcement practices target, not merely the model's arithmetic.

sections.title: Some Defendants Cannot Pay
sections.body_md: A company may cause large injury but hold few collectible assets or enter insolvency. Economists call this a judgment-proof problem: anticipated liability may exceed the actor's available resources. Victims can then remain uncompensated and prevention incentives may weaken. Law may respond through insurance requirements, capital rules or other mechanisms where authorized. Each shifts costs and can affect market entry. A good analysis considers whether the proposed protection is workable rather than assuming every judgment will be satisfied.

sections.title: Who Bears the Remedy's Burden?
sections.body_md: A flat fine may be trivial for a large corporation but severe for a poor individual. A policy can reduce average harm while concentrating enforcement on marginalized communities. Evaluate payment size, ability to comply, available defenses and procedural safeguards. The aim is not to abandon enforcement but to ensure its burden and benefits are justified. Economic evidence is useful when it reveals who really pays and whether the rule protects those most exposed.

black.focus: Defend humane and efficient institutions of legal redress
black.summary: At doctoral depth, combine the economics of incentives with corrective justice, dignity and public accountability. Develop remedial systems that protect rights without assuming all values are convertible into money.
checklist: I can critique optimal-penalty models under unequal enforcement
I can combine prevention, compensation and procedural fairness
I can propose reviewable remedies for systemic harms

sections.title: The Most Efficient Fine May Be Unjust
sections.body_md: A theoretical model might raise penalties sharply when the chance of detection is low. Yet very high sanctions can create devastating errors, incentives for corruption or disproportionate burdens on vulnerable groups. A legal system must consider due process, proportionality, equality and institutional competence. The doctoral question is not only how to change average behavior, but whether the mechanism is lawfully and morally justified for the people it subjects to coercion.

sections.title: Damage Cannot Always Be Undone
sections.body_md: An unlawful removal of a child, loss of liberty or destruction of an irreplaceable ecosystem cannot be fully repaired through a money judgment. Prevention, restoration, acknowledgment and institutional reform can have value alongside compensation. Their availability and powers depend on the governing law. A rigorous reform proposal identifies which losses monetary models omit and which institutions can provide meaningful relief without exceeding legitimate authority.

sections.title: Design Accountability Into the Remedy
sections.body_md: Consider a recurring failure to deliver legally required public services. A response might combine individual remedies, transparent performance standards, review rights and independent monitoring. Each component should have a lawful source, a realistic cost and a defined route for correction. Economic evaluation can test whether outcomes improve; legal principles protect those who are burdened. The purpose of remedial design is not simply to optimize a number but to make justice effective in the lives of actual people.
